records.source: Φῆστος οὖν ἐπιβὰς τῇ ἐπαρχείᾳ μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἀνέβη εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀπὸ Καισαρείας, ἐνεφάνισάν τε αὐτῷ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι τῶν Ἰουδαίων κατὰ τοῦ Παύλου, καὶ παρεκάλουν αὐτὸν αἰτούμενοι χάριν κατ’ αὐτοῦ ὅπως μεταπέμψηται αὐτὸν εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ, ἐνέδραν ποιοῦντες ἀνελεῖν αὐτὸν κατὰ τὴν ὁδόν.
records.gloss: Festus therefore having entered the province after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea, \v 2 made a representation then to him the chief priests and the first of the Jews against Paul, and they were urging him, \v 3 asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, an ambush making to kill him along the way.
pieces: Festus had been in his province only three days when he left Caesarea and went up to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the most prominent Jews laid their charges against Paul before him and kept pressing him.
They asked him for a favor that would harm Paul: to send for him to come to Jerusalem. They meant to lie in wait and kill him on the way.

L.1: So Festus, having entered the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea,
L.2: and the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews brought charges before him against Paul, and they were urging him,
L.3: asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, [while] making an ambush to kill him along the way.

R.1: Festus became governor of the province. Three days later, he went from Caesarea up to Jerusalem.
R.2: There the chief priests and the most important Jewish leaders told him what charges they had against Paul. They kept begging Festus
R.3: to do them a favor. They wanted him to bring Paul to Jerusalem. But they were planning to hide along the road and kill Paul on the way.

decisions.choice: having entered the province: having arrived to take up his office
decisions.reason: Festus had just succeeded Felix (24:27). Within three days he went to Jerusalem, the center of Jewish life in his province.

decisions.choice: the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews: the members of the high council
decisions.reason: These are the same groups who accused Paul before Felix (24:1). In 25:15 Festus calls them the chief priests and elders.

decisions.choice: a favor: a concession from the governor, not the grace of God
decisions.reason: The word usually means God's grace, but here it is a favor asked of a man. The same sense comes in 24:27 and 25:9.

decisions.choice: an ambush: the plot of 23:12-22 renewed
decisions.reason: Two years earlier more than forty men had sworn to kill Paul on the way to the council. The plan to kill him on the road is taken up again.

decisions.choice: Festus became governor of the province
decisions.reason: Readable says what Festus's arrival meant.

decisions.choice: a favor that would harm Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced says plainly how the favor was against him.

records.heading: Festus hears Paul, and Paul appeals to Caesar

records.source: ὁ μὲν οὖν Φῆστος ἀπεκρίθη τηρεῖσθαι τὸν Παῦλον εἰς Καισάρειαν, ἑαυτὸν δὲ μέλλειν ἐν τάχει ἐκπορεύεσθαι·
records.gloss: Festus indeed therefore answered Paul to be kept in Caesarea, himself and to be about in quickness to go out;
pieces: Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be going back there.

L.4: Festus, then, answered that Paul was being kept in Caesarea, and that he himself was about to go [there] shortly.

R.4: Festus told them that Paul was being kept in Caesarea, and that he himself would be going back there soon.

decisions.choice: was being kept: Paul would stay where he was
decisions.reason: The present tense describes the present state of things. Festus turns down the request without saying so directly.

decisions.choice: then: in answer to the request
decisions.reason: The two small words mark Festus's reply as the next step, and they prepare for his offer in 25:5.

decisions.choice: going back there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where Festus was going.

records.source: Οἱ οὖν ἐν ὑμῖν, φησίν, δυνατοὶ συγκαταβάντες εἴ τί ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ἀνδρὶ ἄτοπον κατηγορείτωσαν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Those therefore among you, he says, powerful having gone down with, if anything is in the man out of place, let them accuse him.
pieces: "So let your leading men travel down with me," he said, "and if there is anything improper about this man, they can accuse him there."

L.5: "So," he says, "let those among you who are in authority go down with [me], and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him."

R.5: He said, "Your leaders can come with me to Caesarea. If this man has done something wrong, they can accuse him there."

decisions.choice: those in authority: the leaders
alternatives: those who are able to travel
decisions.reason: The word means the powerful, or those able to do something. Since the chief priests and leading men had asked, it fits their leaders best.

decisions.choice: wrong: improper, out of place
decisions.reason: The word means out of place, unfitting. Festus speaks without assuming a serious crime (compare 28:6).

decisions.choice: he says: the present tense in a story
decisions.reason: Luke sometimes uses the present tense for a speaker's words, to make the scene vivid.

decisions.choice: there; to Caesarea
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say where the trial would be.

records.source: Διατρίψας δὲ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡμέρας οὐ πλείους ὀκτὼ ἢ δέκα, καταβὰς εἰς Καισάρειαν, τῇ ἐπαύριον καθίσας ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος ἐκέλευσεν τὸν Παῦλον ἀχθῆναι.
records.gloss: Having stayed then among them days not more than eight or ten, having gone down to Caesarea, on the next day having sat on the judgment seat he ordered Paul to be brought.
pieces: He spent no more than eight or ten days with them and then went down to Caesarea. The day after he arrived, he took his place on the judgment seat and had Paul brought in.

L.6: And having spent among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea; on the next day, having sat on the judgment seat, he ordered Paul to be brought.

R.6: Festus stayed in Jerusalem eight or ten days, not more. Then he went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat down in the judge's seat and ordered that Paul be brought in.

decisions.choice: the judgment seat: the raised seat from which a Roman official gave judgment
decisions.reason: Taking this seat made the hearing a formal session of the governor's court (compare 18:12; 25:10, 25:17).

decisions.choice: on the next day: without delay after his return
decisions.reason: Festus himself stresses this in 25:17: he lost no time.

decisions.choice: the judge's seat
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the official seat.

records.source: παραγενομένου δὲ αὐτοῦ περιέστησαν αὐτὸν οἱ ἀπὸ Ἱεροσολύμων καταβεβηκότες Ἰουδαῖοι, πολλὰ καὶ βαρέα αἰτιώματα καταφέροντες ἃ οὐκ ἴσχυον ἀποδεῖξαι, τοῦ Παύλου ἀπολογουμένου ὅτι Οὔτε εἰς τὸν νόμον τῶν Ἰουδαίων οὔτε εἰς τὸ ἱερὸν οὔτε εἰς Καίσαρά τι ἥμαρτον.
records.gloss: Having arrived then him stood around him the from Jerusalem having come down Jews, many and weighty charges bringing which not they were able to prove, \v 8 Paul defending himself that, Neither against the law of the Jews nor against the temple nor against Caesar anything have I sinned.
pieces: As soon as Paul appeared, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem crowded around him and laid many heavy charges on him, none of which they could prove.
Paul's defense was this: "I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar."

L.7: And when he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and weighty charges which they were not able to prove,
L.8: while Paul said in his defense, "Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I sinned in anything."

R.7: When Paul came in, the Jewish leaders from Jerusalem stood all around him. They said he had done many terrible things, but they could not prove any of it.
R.8: Then Paul defended himself. He said, "I have not done anything wrong against the Jewish law, or against the temple, or against Caesar, the Roman emperor."

decisions.choice: when he had arrived: Paul
decisions.reason: Paul had just been ordered to be brought in (25:6).

decisions.choice: three charges: against the law, the temple and Caesar
decisions.reason: Paul answers the three kinds of charge brought against him: breaking the Jewish law, defiling the temple (21:28; 24:6), and stirring up trouble against Roman rule (17:7; 24:5).

decisions.choice: Caesar: the Roman emperor
decisions.reason: Caesar had become a title of the emperors. The emperor at this time was Nero.

decisions.choice: sinned: done wrong, committed an offense
decisions.reason: The verb is used here of wrongs against the law and against the emperor, so it means any offense.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the man who arrived.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders from Jerusalem
alternatives: the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable names who these Jews were: the chief priests and leading men who accused Paul before Festus in Jerusalem (25:2) and whom he invited to come down with him (25:5).

decisions.choice: Caesar, the Roman emperor
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title the first time it comes in the chapter.

records.source: ὁ Φῆστος δὲ θέλων τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις χάριν καταθέσθαι ἀποκριθεὶς τῷ Παύλῳ εἶπεν· Θέλεις εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀναβὰς ἐκεῖ περὶ τούτων κριθῆναι ἐπ’ ἐμοῦ;
records.gloss: Festus however wishing to the Jews a favor to lay up, answering Paul said, Are you willing to Jerusalem having gone up there concerning these things to be judged before me?
pieces: Festus, though, was looking to build up favor with the Jews. He turned to Paul and said, "Would you agree to go up to Jerusalem and have these matters judged there, with me presiding?"

L.9: But Festus, wishing to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and there be judged before me concerning these things?"

R.9: But Festus wanted to win the favor of the Jewish leaders. So he asked Paul, "Are you willing to go to Jerusalem? I would judge your case there."

decisions.choice: favor: goodwill from people, not the grace of God
decisions.reason: As in 24:27, where Felix did the same, the word means human goodwill that Festus hoped to store up.

decisions.choice: before me: Festus would still be the judge
decisions.reason: Festus offers to hear the case himself in Jerusalem. Even so, the move would put Paul back in the city where his enemies planned to kill him (25:3).

decisions.choice: are you willing: Festus asks Paul's consent
decisions.reason: Festus does not order the move. Luke does not say why he asked; Paul's answer refuses.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Readable names the people Festus wanted to please, the accusers of 25:2 and 25:7.

records.source: εἶπεν δὲ ὁ Παῦλος· Ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος Καίσαρος ἑστώς εἰμι, οὗ με δεῖ κρίνεσθαι.
records.gloss: Said then Paul, Before the judgment seat of Caesar standing I am, where me it is necessary to be judged.
pieces: Paul said, "The court I stand before is Caesar's, and here is where my case belongs.

L.10: And Paul said, "I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be judged.

R.10: Paul answered, "I am standing in Caesar's court right now. This is the court that should judge me.

decisions.choice: the judgment seat of Caesar: the court of the Roman governor, who judged in the emperor's name
alternatives: the emperor's own court in Rome
decisions.reason: Festus held his authority from the emperor, so his court was Caesar's court.

decisions.choice: ought: it is right, as a matter of law
decisions.reason: Paul is a Roman citizen (22:25-29). A Roman court is the proper place for his case, not a Jewish one.

decisions.choice: here is where my case belongs
alternatives: where I ought to be judged
decisions.reason: Balanced puts Paul's legal claim in natural English.

records.source: Ἰουδαίους οὐδὲν ἠδίκησα, ὡς καὶ σὺ κάλλιον ἐπιγινώσκεις.
records.gloss: To Jews nothing I have wronged, as also you very well know.
pieces: I have wronged the Jews in nothing, and you know this quite well yourself.

L.10: To [the] Jews I have done no wrong, as you also know very well.

R.10: I have not done anything wrong to the Jews. You know that very well.

decisions.choice: very well: better than you are showing
decisions.reason: The word is a comparative, "better". It may only mean "very well", but it may also hint that Festus knows more than his offer in 25:9 suggests.

decisions.choice: done wrong: committed an injustice
decisions.reason: The verb means to act unjustly toward someone. Paul repeats the word in 25:11.

records.source: εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀδικῶ καὶ ἄξιον θανάτου πέπραχά τι, οὐ παραιτοῦμαι τὸ ἀποθανεῖν· εἰ δὲ οὐδέν ἐστιν ὧν οὗτοι κατηγοροῦσίν μου, οὐδείς με δύναται αὐτοῖς χαρίσασθαι· Καίσαρα ἐπικαλοῦμαι.
records.gloss: If indeed therefore I do wrong and worthy of death have done anything, not I refuse to die; if however nothing there is of which these accuse me, no one me is able to them to hand over; to Caesar I appeal.
pieces: If I am guilty and have done something for which I deserve to die, I do not ask to be spared death. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar!"

L.11: If then I am a wrongdoer and have done anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die; but if there is nothing [in the things] of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar."

R.11: If I have done something wrong, something that deserves death, I am not trying to escape death. But if their charges are not true, no one can give me to them just to please them. I appeal to Caesar! Let the emperor himself judge my case."

decisions.choice: hand over: give up as a favor
decisions.reason: The verb is related to the word for favor and means to grant something freely. Paul answers Festus's wish to do the Jews a favor (25:9): no one may make him a present to them. Festus uses the same verb in 25:16.

decisions.choice: I appeal to Caesar: a Roman citizen's right to have his case heard by the emperor
decisions.reason: A Roman citizen could appeal from a governor's court to the emperor. Once he did, the governor had to send him on (25:12, 25:21; 26:32).

decisions.choice: I am a wrongdoer: if I am in the wrong
alternatives: if I am doing wrong now
decisions.reason: The present tense describes Paul's standing before the law: whether he is guilty.

decisions.choice: hand me over to them as a favor
decisions.reason: Balanced shows the link with the favor of 25:9, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: Let the emperor himself judge my case
decisions.reason: Readable explains what an appeal to Caesar meant.

records.source: τότε ὁ Φῆστος συλλαλήσας μετὰ τοῦ συμβουλίου ἀπεκρίθη· Καίσαρα ἐπικέκλησαι, ἐπὶ Καίσαρα πορεύσῃ.
records.gloss: Then Festus having conferred with the council answered, To Caesar you have appealed, to Caesar you will go.
pieces: Then Festus talked it over with his advisers and replied, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go."

L.12: Then Festus, having conferred with the council, answered, "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go."

R.12: Festus talked with his advisers. Then he said to Paul, "You have asked for Caesar to judge you. So you will go to Caesar."

decisions.choice: the council: the governor's group of advisers
decisions.reason: Roman officials took advice from a council of their own staff before ruling on a case. This is a different word from the Jewish council of 24:20.

decisions.choice: You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go: a formal ruling
decisions.reason: The repeated name makes a solemn ruling. Festus accepts the appeal.

decisions.choice: his advisers
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid confusion with the Jewish council.

records.source: Ἡμερῶν δὲ διαγενομένων τινῶν Ἀγρίππας ὁ βασιλεὺς καὶ Βερνίκη κατήντησαν εἰς Καισάρειαν ἀσπασάμενοι τὸν Φῆστον.
records.gloss: Days then having passed some, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea having greeted Festus.
pieces: After some days had gone by, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea on a visit of welcome to Festus.

L.13: Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea, greeting Festus.

R.13: Some days later, King Agrippa and his sister Bernice came to Caesarea. They came to welcome Festus as the new governor.

decisions.choice: Agrippa the king: Herod Agrippa II, son of the Herod of 12:1-23
decisions.reason: Agrippa II ruled lands to the north and east of Galilee under Rome. He also had charge of the temple and appointed the high priests (Josephus, Antiquities 20.222).

decisions.choice: Bernice: Agrippa's sister
decisions.reason: Bernice was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I and a sister of Drusilla (24:24). Josephus says she lived with her brother at this time (Antiquities 20.145).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "having greeted", the visit itself as the greeting
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts have the future participle, "in order to greet", which is the easier reading. The SBLGNT has the past tense form. The sense is much the same: the visit was a courtesy call. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: his sister; as the new governor
decisions.reason: Readable says who Bernice was and why they came.

records.heading: Festus lays Paul's case before King Agrippa

records.source: ὡς δὲ πλείους ἡμέρας διέτριβον ἐκεῖ, ὁ Φῆστος τῷ βασιλεῖ ἀνέθετο τὰ κατὰ τὸν Παῦλον λέγων· Ἀνήρ τίς ἐστιν καταλελειμμένος ὑπὸ Φήλικος δέσμιος, περὶ οὗ γενομένου μου εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἐνεφάνισαν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τῶν Ἰουδαίων, αἰτούμενοι κατ’ αὐτοῦ καταδίκην·
records.gloss: As then many days they were staying there, Festus to the king laid out the things concerning Paul saying, A man certain there is left behind by Felix a prisoner, \v 15 concerning whom, having been me in Jerusalem, made a representation the chief priests and the elders of the Jews, asking against him condemnation;
pieces: Their visit lasted many days, and during it Festus told the king about Paul. "Felix left a certain man behind in custody," he said.
"When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the Jewish elders laid information against him and asked me to condemn him.

L.14: And as they were staying there many days, Festus laid out Paul's case before the king, saying, "There is a certain man left behind by Felix as a prisoner,
L.15: concerning whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought charges, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him.

R.14: They stayed there many days. During that time Festus told the king about Paul's case. He said, "When Felix left, there was a man he kept in prison here.
R.15: When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the Jewish elders told me what charges they had against him. They asked me to say that he was guilty.

decisions.choice: laid out: set a matter before someone for advice
decisions.reason: The verb means to lay something before another person to consult him (Galatians 2:2). Agrippa knew Jewish matters (26:3).

decisions.choice: a sentence of condemnation: a guilty verdict
decisions.reason: The word means a judgment against someone. The leaders wanted Paul condemned without a trial.

decisions.choice: brought charges: made a formal accusation
decisions.reason: The same legal verb as 24:1 and 25:2.

decisions.choice: two quoted sentences with "he said" between them
decisions.reason: Balanced breaks Festus's long sentence into two.

records.source: πρὸς οὓς ἀπεκρίθην ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἔθος Ῥωμαίοις χαρίζεσθαί τινα ἄνθρωπον πρὶν ἢ ὁ κατηγορούμενος κατὰ πρόσωπον ἔχοι τοὺς κατηγόρους τόπον τε ἀπολογίας λάβοι περὶ τοῦ ἐγκλήματος.
records.gloss: to whom I answered that not it is a custom to Romans to hand over any man before the [one] being accused face to face may have the accusers, opportunity and of defense may receive concerning the charge.
pieces: I told them that it is not the Roman way to give anyone up as a favor until the accused person has met the accusers face to face and been given a chance to answer the charge.

L.16: To them I answered that it is not [the] custom of [the] Romans to hand over any {{gender:person|man}} before the accused has the accusers face to face and receives an opportunity for a defense concerning the charge.

R.16: I told them, 'That is not how we Romans do things. We do not give a person up to be punished just to please someone. First that person must meet the accusers face to face, and must have a chance to answer their charges.'

decisions.choice: a Roman principle: the accused faces the accusers and may answer
decisions.reason: Roman law held that no one should be condemned without hearing, with the accuser present. Festus presents his handling of the case as fair.

decisions.choice: hand over: give up as a favor
decisions.reason: The same verb Paul used in 25:11. Festus says he would not make a gift of a prisoner to his accusers.

decisions.choice: any person: anyone at all
decisions.reason: The word means a human being. Festus states a general rule.

decisions.choice: person, with "man" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word means a person of either sex; the traditional rendering is the alternative.

decisions.choice: Festus's answer as a quotation inside his speech
decisions.reason: Readable turns the reported answer into words Festus spoke, in single quotation marks inside his speech.

decisions.choice: as a favor; just to please someone
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show the sense of giving someone up as a favor, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: συνελθόντων οὖν ἐνθάδε ἀναβολὴν μηδεμίαν ποιησάμενος τῇ ἑξῆς καθίσας ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος ἐκέλευσα ἀχθῆναι τὸν ἄνδρα·
records.gloss: Having come together therefore here, delay no having made, on the next [day] having sat on the judgment seat I ordered to be brought the man;
pieces: So when they had come here with me, I lost no time. The very next day I took my place on the judgment seat and had the man brought in.

L.17: So when they had come together here, I made no delay; on the next [day] I sat on the judgment seat and ordered the man to be brought.

R.17: So when they came here, I did not wait. The next day I sat down in the judge's seat and ordered that the man be brought in.

decisions.choice: they had come together: the accusers came to Caesarea
decisions.reason: This refers to the leaders who came down from Jerusalem with Festus (25:5-7).

decisions.choice: I made no delay: a point of good government
decisions.reason: Festus stresses his promptness, in contrast to the two years of delay under Felix.

decisions.choice: the judge's seat
decisions.reason: As in 25:6.

records.source: περὶ οὗ σταθέντες οἱ κατήγοροι οὐδεμίαν αἰτίαν ἔφερον ὧν ἐγὼ ὑπενόουν πονηρῶν, ζητήματα δέ τινα περὶ τῆς ἰδίας δεισιδαιμονίας εἶχον πρὸς αὐτὸν καὶ περί τινος Ἰησοῦ τεθνηκότος, ὃν ἔφασκεν ὁ Παῦλος ζῆν.
records.gloss: concerning whom having stood the accusers no charge were bringing of the things I was suspecting evil, \v 19 questions however certain concerning their own religion they had against him and concerning a certain Jesus having died, whom was asserting Paul to be alive.
pieces: His accusers stood up, but the charges they brought were not the crimes I had been expecting.
What they had against him were certain questions about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul asserted to be alive.

L.18: When the accusers stood up concerning him, they were bringing no charge of the evil things I was suspecting,
L.19: but they had certain questions against him about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul was asserting to be alive.

R.18: His accusers stood up to speak. But they did not accuse him of any of the crimes I had expected.
R.19: Instead, they argued with him about their own religion. They also argued about a man named Jesus, who had died. But Paul kept saying that Jesus is alive.

decisions.choice: evil things: crimes
decisions.reason: Festus expected charges of real crimes under Roman law, such as rioting or sedition (24:5).

decisions.choice: religion: the Jewish faith and worship
decisions.reason: The word can mean reverence for the gods or superstition. Speaking to Agrippa, a Jewish king, Festus would hardly mean an insult. Paul used the related adjective of the Athenians (17:22).

decisions.choice: a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul asserted to be alive: Festus's outsider's summary
decisions.reason: Festus speaks of Jesus as an unknown man and sums up the dispute as a dead man said to be alive. The verb "was asserting" is in a tense of repeated action: Paul kept saying it. Without knowing it, Festus names the center of Paul's preaching, the resurrection (17:31; 26:23).

decisions.choice: that Jesus is alive
decisions.reason: Readable names Jesus again so that the sentence is clear.

records.source: ἀπορούμενος δὲ ἐγὼ τὴν περὶ τούτων ζήτησιν ἔλεγον εἰ βούλοιτο πορεύεσθαι εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα κἀκεῖ κρίνεσθαι περὶ τούτων.
records.gloss: Being at a loss then I concerning these things inquiry, was saying if he would wish to go to Jerusalem and there to be judged concerning these things.
pieces: I was unsure how to go about investigating questions like these, and so I asked whether he would like to go to Jerusalem and have the matter judged there.

L.20: And I, being at a loss about the inquiry into these things, asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these things.

R.20: I did not know how to look into questions like these. So I asked Paul if he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about these things.

decisions.choice: being at a loss: not knowing how to proceed
decisions.reason: The verb means to be without a way forward, perplexed.

decisions.choice: Festus's account leaves out his own motive
decisions.reason: Luke has told the reader that Festus asked this to win favor with the Jews (25:9). To Agrippa he gives only his uncertainty about Jewish questions.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Readable names the one Festus asked.

records.source: τοῦ δὲ Παύλου ἐπικαλεσαμένου τηρηθῆναι αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν τοῦ Σεβαστοῦ διάγνωσιν, ἐκέλευσα τηρεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ἕως οὗ ἀναπέμψω αὐτὸν πρὸς Καίσαρα.
records.gloss: Paul however having appealed to be kept him for the of the Revered One decision, I ordered to be kept him until I might send up him to Caesar.
pieces: But Paul appealed to be held for the emperor's decision, so I ordered him to be kept in custody until I can send him on to Caesar."

L.21: But when Paul had appealed to be kept [in custody] for the decision of His Majesty, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar."

R.21: But Paul asked to be kept in prison until the emperor himself could decide his case. So I ordered that he be kept here until I can send him to Caesar."

decisions.choice: the Revered One: the emperor's title of honor, the Greek form of Augustus
decisions.reason: The word means revered or worthy of worship. It translates the Latin title Augustus, given to the first emperor and borne by every emperor after him. Here it means the reigning emperor, Nero, as Caesar does. Luke uses it only here and in 25:25; in 27:1 the same word names an army unit.

decisions.choice: decision: a judicial hearing and verdict
decisions.reason: The word means a legal examination and decision. Paul asked to be judged by the emperor's court.

decisions.choice: send: send up to a higher authority
decisions.reason: The verb is used of sending a case on to a higher court (compare Luke 23:7, 23:11, 23:15).

decisions.choice: His Majesty
decisions.reason: Literal uses an English title of honor so that the reader sees a title, not the name of the first emperor, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: the emperor
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say who is meant.

records.source: Ἀγρίππας δὲ πρὸς τὸν Φῆστον· Ἐβουλόμην καὶ αὐτὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀκοῦσαι.
records.gloss: Agrippa then to Festus, I was wishing also myself the man to hear.
pieces: Agrippa told Festus, "I have been wanting to hear the man for myself."

L.22: And Agrippa [said] to Festus, "I myself was also wishing to hear the man."

R.22: Agrippa said to Festus, "I want to hear what this man says, too."

decisions.choice: I was wishing: a polite present wish, or a wish he had held for some time
alternatives: a wish he had given up
decisions.reason: The past tense of this verb can be a polite way to say "I would like". It can also mean that Agrippa had wanted to hear Paul for a while.

decisions.choice: to Festus: the verb of saying is left out
decisions.reason: The Greek leaves out "said", as often in quick dialogue.

decisions.choice: told; said
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb without brackets.

records.source: Αὔριον, φησίν, ἀκούσῃ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Tomorrow, he says, you will hear him.
pieces: "You will hear him tomorrow," Festus replied.

R.22: Festus said, "You will hear him tomorrow."

decisions.choice: he says: Festus answers
decisions.reason: The present tense makes the reply vivid, as in 25:5. The speaker is Festus.

decisions.choice: Festus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

records.source: Τῇ οὖν ἐπαύριον ἐλθόντος τοῦ Ἀγρίππα καὶ τῆς Βερνίκης μετὰ πολλῆς φαντασίας καὶ εἰσελθόντων εἰς τὸ ἀκροατήριον σύν τε χιλιάρχοις καὶ ἀνδράσιν τοῖς κατ’ ἐξοχὴν τῆς πόλεως καὶ κελεύσαντος τοῦ Φήστου ἤχθη ὁ Παῦλος.
records.gloss: On the next day therefore having come Agrippa and Bernice with much pomp and having entered into the audience hall with both tribunes and men the in prominence of the city, and having ordered Festus, was brought Paul.
pieces: So the following day Agrippa and Bernice came with a great show of splendor. They went into the hall of hearing along with the tribunes and the city's most important men, and Festus gave the order for Paul to be brought.

L.23: So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp and had entered the audience hall with both the tribunes and the men of prominence in the city, at Festus's order Paul was brought in.

R.23: The next day Agrippa and Bernice arrived with a grand parade, to show how important they were. They went into the large meeting room with the tribunes, who commanded the soldiers, and with the most important men of the city. Then Festus gave an order, and Paul was brought in.

decisions.choice: great pomp: a showy display of rank
decisions.reason: The word means a display or show. It describes the royal ceremony with which Agrippa and Bernice came.

decisions.choice: the audience hall: a room for hearings and audiences
decisions.reason: The word comes from the verb to hear. It was a hall in the governor's residence where cases and petitions were heard.

decisions.choice: tribunes: the commanders of the troops stationed at Caesarea
decisions.reason: A tribune commanded a cohort of soldiers (21:31). Several cohorts were based at Caesarea, the seat of the governor.

decisions.choice: a grand parade, to show how important they were
decisions.reason: Readable explains what pomp was.

decisions.choice: the tribunes, who commanded the soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title.

records.source: καί φησιν ὁ Φῆστος· Ἀγρίππα βασιλεῦ καὶ πάντες οἱ συμπαρόντες ἡμῖν ἄνδρες, θεωρεῖτε τοῦτον περὶ οὗ ἅπαν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐνέτυχόν μοι ἔν τε Ἱεροσολύμοις καὶ ἐνθάδε, βοῶντες μὴ δεῖν αὐτὸν ζῆν μηκέτι.
records.gloss: And says Festus, Agrippa King and all the being present with us men, you see this one concerning whom all the multitude of the Jews pleaded with me both in Jerusalem and here, crying out not he ought to live any longer.
pieces: Then Festus spoke: "King Agrippa, and all {{gender:of you|you men}} who are here with us, look at this man. The entire Jewish people has come to me about him, in Jerusalem and here too, shouting that he has no right to go on living.

L.24: And Festus says, "King Agrippa and all [you] men present with us, you see this man concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.

R.24: Festus said, "King Agrippa, and all {{gender:of you|you men}} here with us, look at this man. All the Jewish people have come to me and complained about him. They did this in Jerusalem, and they did it here too. They shouted that he should be put to death.

decisions.choice: men: a formal address to the gathering
decisions.reason: The hearers were mostly men, the tribunes and leading men of the city (25:23), but Bernice was also present. The address is the customary formal one and may include everyone in the hall.

decisions.choice: the whole multitude of the Jews: an overstatement
decisions.reason: In fact the accusers were the chief priests and leading men (25:2, 25:7, 25:15). Festus makes the pressure on him sound as great as possible.

decisions.choice: petitioned: made an appeal to an official
decisions.reason: The verb means to approach someone with a request or a complaint.

decisions.choice: all of you, with "all you men" as the alternative
decisions.reason: As the meaning note explains, the address may include everyone present. Literal keeps the Greek word.

decisions.choice: he should be put to death
alternatives: he ought not to live any longer
decisions.reason: Readable states the demand plainly.

records.source: ἐγὼ δὲ κατελαβόμην μηδὲν ἄξιον αὐτὸν θανάτου πεπραχέναι, αὐτοῦ δὲ τούτου ἐπικαλεσαμένου τὸν Σεβαστὸν ἔκρινα πέμπειν.
records.gloss: I however found nothing worthy him of death to have done, himself and this one having appealed to the Revered One I decided to send.
pieces: I, for my part, saw that he had committed no crime that merits death. And as he has made an appeal to the emperor himself, I resolved to send him on.

L.25: But I found that he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he himself appealed to His Majesty, I decided to send [him].

R.25: But I could see that he had done nothing that deserved death. And he asked the emperor to judge his case. So I decided to send him to the emperor.

decisions.choice: nothing worthy of death: another Roman finding of innocence
decisions.reason: Lysias had found the same (23:29), and Agrippa and Festus will agree again (26:31-32). Luke shows that Roman officials found no crime in Paul.

decisions.choice: the Revered One: the emperor
decisions.reason: The same title as in 25:21: the reigning emperor.

decisions.choice: His Majesty
decisions.reason: As in 25:21.

decisions.choice: the emperor
decisions.reason: As in 25:21.

records.source: περὶ οὗ ἀσφαλές τι γράψαι τῷ κυρίῳ οὐκ ἔχω· διὸ προήγαγον αὐτὸν ἐφ’ ὑμῶν καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ σοῦ, βασιλεῦ Ἀγρίππα, ὅπως τῆς ἀνακρίσεως γενομένης σχῶ τί γράψω·
records.gloss: concerning whom anything certain to write to the lord not I have; therefore I brought forth him before you and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that the examination having taken place I might have something I might write.
pieces: Yet I have nothing solid to put in a letter about him to my lord. That is why I have brought him out here before you all, King Agrippa, you above all, so that once he has been examined I may have something I can write.

L.26: But I have nothing definite to write to [my] lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you [all], and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after the examination has taken place, I may have something to write.

R.26: But I do not know what to write about him to the emperor. That is why I have brought him here to all of you, and most of all to you, King Agrippa. After you have questioned him, I hope I will have something to write.

decisions.choice: the lord: the emperor, as master of the empire
decisions.reason: Here the word is a title for the emperor, not a name for God. Calling the emperor lord was common in the east by this time. Later Christians were pressed to say "Caesar is lord" and refused (Martyrdom of Polycarp 8.2).

decisions.choice: the examination: a preliminary hearing
decisions.reason: The related verb is used of judicial questioning (4:9; 12:19; 24:8). This hearing would decide nothing; it would only help Festus write his report.

decisions.choice: before you all: the whole gathering
decisions.reason: The plural "you" addresses the whole gathering; then Festus turns to Agrippa in the singular.

decisions.choice: lord, in lower case
decisions.reason: The capital letter is kept for God and Jesus. Here the title belongs to the emperor.

decisions.choice: the emperor
decisions.reason: Readable says who is meant.

decisions.choice: I hope
decisions.reason: Readable turns the purpose clause into a plain hope.

records.source: ἄλογον γάρ μοι δοκεῖ πέμποντα δέσμιον μὴ καὶ τὰς κατ’ αὐτοῦ αἰτίας σημᾶναι.
records.gloss: Unreasonable for to me it seems, sending a prisoner, not also the against him charges to indicate.
pieces: For to send a prisoner and not make clear what he is charged with seems senseless to me."

L.27: For it seems unreasonable to me, in sending a prisoner, not also to indicate the charges against him."

R.27: I think it would be foolish to send a prisoner to the emperor without saying what he is accused of."

decisions.choice: the charges: a governor sending a prisoner on appeal had to send a written report
decisions.reason: A governor who sent a case to the emperor sent a letter setting out the case, as Lysias did when he sent Paul to Felix (23:26-30).

decisions.choice: unreasonable: without sense, absurd
decisions.reason: The word means without reason. Festus admits he has no clear case to report.

decisions.choice: to the emperor
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom the prisoner was being sent.
